defaults.permitted_development: A hard surface for a driveway at a house in Scotland is usually permitted development if it is incidental to the house. Where the surface lies between the dwellinghouse and a road, the materials should be permeable or rainwater should drain to porous ground within the curtilage. A separate roads consent for a new access or footway crossing may still be needed, and these householder rights do not apply to flats.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate national driveway height allowance. Ramps, retaining walls, steps and major level changes are assessed as part of the wider works.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth limit. The main checks are whether the surfacing remains incidental to the house and whether drainage is handled properly.
rules.boundary_rules: Creating vehicular access across a public footway or verge needs roads authority consent, and planning permission may also be needed where the access is onto a classified road or other restrictions apply.
rules.roof_rules: Driveway surfacing creates no separate roof right. Car ports, canopies and garages are separate forms of development.
rules.materials_rules: Where the hard surface lies between the dwellinghouse and a road, the materials should be permeable or rainwater should drain to porous ground within the curtilage. Keeping water off the public road is the safest design approach.

rules.permitted_development: A hard surface for a driveway at a house in Scotland is often permitted development if it is incidental to the house. In more urban streets, though, that does not remove the need for a roads authority decision on any new crossover and a planning check where access is onto a classified road.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate national driveway height allowance. Ramps, retaining walls, steps and major level changes are assessed as part of the wider works.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth rule. The layout should still allow a vehicle to stand on the site and manoeuvre safely without routinely blocking the footway.
rules.boundary_rules: Creating vehicular access across a public footway or verge needs roads authority consent. In built-up areas, visibility, parking controls, street furniture and drainage standards can be decisive even where the surfacing itself is minor.
rules.roof_rules: Driveway surfacing creates no separate roof right. Car ports, canopies and garages are separate forms of development.
rules.materials_rules: Where the hard surface lies between the dwellinghouse and a road, the materials should be permeable or rainwater should drain to porous ground within the curtilage. The private drive should also be set up so water does not run onto the public road.

restrictions.conservation_area: In a conservation area in Scotland, normal householder permitted development rights for new hard surfaces can be curtailed where associated boundary or access works affect character, so a planning check is sensible before work starts.
restrictions.listed_building: There are no ordinary householder permitted development rights for works within the curtilage of a listed building where they would affect its character, and listed building consent may also be required.

Where the surface lies between the dwellinghouse and a road, the materials should be permeable or rainwater should drain to porous ground within the curtilage. A separate roads consent for a new access or footway crossing may still be needed, and these householder rights do not apply to flats.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate national driveway height allowance. Ramps, retaining walls, steps and major level changes are assessed as part of the wider works.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth limit. The main checks are whether the surfacing remains incidental to the house and whether drainage is handled properly.
rules.boundary_rules: Creating vehicular access across a public footway or verge needs roads authority consent, and planning permission may also be needed where the access is onto a classified road or other restrictions apply.
rules.roof_rules: Driveway surfacing creates no separate roof right. Car ports, canopies and garages are separate forms of development.

rules.permitted_development: A domestic hard surface in Scotland can still be permitted development in a national park, but the planning risk usually lies in associated access works, boundary removal and whether the finished scheme looks engineered rather than incidental to the house.

rules.height_rules: There is no special driveway height allowance. Significant cutting into slopes, retaining walls or raised platforms can make the proposal more than a simple hard surface.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth limit, but broad parking aprons and engineered platforms are more likely to raise landscape and design concerns in protected areas.
rules.boundary_rules: Creating vehicular access across a public footway or verge needs roads authority consent, and planning permission may also be needed where the access is onto a classified road or other restrictions apply.
rules.roof_rules: Driveway rules do not cover covered parking or shelters. Any roofed structure is a separate development question.
rules.materials_rules: Use permeable surfacing and quiet, recessive finishes. Overly urban kerbs, bright block paving and extensive edging are more likely to look out of place in a national park setting.
